# Overview

The proposal planned to explain high-surprisal tokens with delta vectors,
δ = e_pred − e_obs in OLMo-2 1B's output space, decomposed by NMF. This
appendix reports that analysis and why it does not answer the question. It
rests on two premises, checked first.

1. The token-level surprisal used here is the same quantity Study 1 validated
   and Study 2 placed in the nomological network.
2. δ carries information about *how the prediction failed*, not just *which
   word was observed*. If δ is mostly a function of the observed word, an NMF
   of δ will recover a vocabulary partition.

The second premise fails, by construction, and the decomposition then does
what that predicts. Inputs come from `1_extract.py`, `2_select.py` and
`appendix/A1`–`A6`. Every estimate uses ELLIPSE dev essays unless a table says
otherwise. Units are bits. The analysis rules were frozen before the test set
was read (`DECISIONS.md`, D11).

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)

source("src/1-predictability-benchmark/_viz_helpers.R")
RESULTS <- "results/study3"
R3 <- RESULTS
TH <- fromJSON(file.path(RESULTS, "threshold.json"))
BANDS <- c("low", "mid", "high")
labels <- read_csv("src/3-surprisal-decomposition/appendix/component_labels.csv")
comps <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "components_delta.csv")) |> left_join(select(labels, -top_lemma_share), by = "component")
cors_test <- read_csv(file.path(R3, "component_correlations_test.csv")) |> left_join(select(labels, -top_lemma_share), by = "component")
sweep <- list.files(R3, "^nmf_ksweep_\\d+\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE) |> map_dfr(read_csv)
```

# 1. The token-level surprisal reproduces Study 1

The extraction pass runs the Study 1 `Predictor` with the same model revision,
dtype, batch size and window, and records the top-50 next-token distribution at
every scored position. The surprisal is recomputed from the same logits the
top-50 comes from, so δ is computed at exactly the prediction that was
thresholded.

```{r}
#| label: reproduction
bind_rows(lapply(names(TH$checks), function(c) as_tibble(TH$checks[[c]]) |> mutate(corpus = c))) |>
  select(corpus, everything()) |>
  kable(digits = 20, caption = "Per-essay agreement with the Study 1 table (window 8)")
```

Agreement is exact up to floating-point summation order. Every essay is
present and every token count matches.

# 2. Threshold and selection

```{r}
#| label: threshold
tibble(
  quantity = c("τ (bits)", "Reference set", "Reference essays", "Reference tokens",
               "ELLIPSE tokens scored", "ELLIPSE tokens selected", "Share selected",
               "Selected, dev", "Selected, test"),
  value = c(sprintf("%.3f", TH$tau_bits),
            sprintf("dev essays with Overall ≥ %.1f", TH$dev_top_tertile_overall_cut),
            format(TH$n_reference_essays, big.mark = ","),
            format(TH$n_reference_tokens, big.mark = ","),
            format(TH$exclusions$ellipse$n_scored, big.mark = ","),
            format(TH$exclusions$ellipse$n_selected, big.mark = ","),
            sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * TH$exclusions$ellipse$n_selected / TH$exclusions$ellipse$n_scored),
            format(TH$n_selected_by_split$dev, big.mark = ","),
            format(TH$n_selected_by_split$test, big.mark = ","))
) |> kable(caption = "Threshold definition and counts")
```

Overall is reported in half-points, so the "top tertile" is every dev essay at
3.5 or above. That is 37% of dev essays, not 33%. A threshold of 11.3 bits
means the model gave the observed word a probability below about 1 in 2,500.

## How the selected tokens spread over proficiency

```{r}
#| label: topk
topk <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "premise_topk.csv")) |>
  mutate(band = factor(band, BANDS)) |> arrange(band)
kable(topk, digits = 3,
      col.names = c("Tertile", "Tokens selected", "Observed in top 50",
                    "Top-50 mass", "Median surprisal", "Mean p(top 1)"),
      caption = "Selected tokens by Overall tertile (all ELLIPSE essays)")
```

The tertiles contribute about equally to the selected set. Low-proficiency
essays have a higher *rate* of high-surprisal tokens, but high-proficiency
essays are longer, and the two roughly cancel. A decomposition fitted to these
rows is therefore not a decomposition of weak writing. A third of its input
comes from the strongest essays in the corpus.

The observed word is almost never among the model's 50 most probable
continuations (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * weighted.mean(topk[[3]], topk[[2]]))` of selected
positions). At these positions, the prediction and the observation are not
near-competitors in the same paradigm. The model was expecting something of a
different kind.

## Composition by part of speech

```{r}
#| label: composition
comp <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "premise_composition.csv")) |>
  mutate(band = factor(band, BANDS))
comp |>
  filter(level == "pos") |>
  select(set, band, pos, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(set, band), values_from = share, values_fill = 0) |>
  arrange(desc(high_low)) |>
  slice_head(n = 12) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Share of tokens by POS, all scored tokens vs. selected tokens, by tertile")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-composition
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
p <- comp |>
  filter(level == "pos", pos %in% c("NOUN", "VERB", "ADJ", "ADV", "PRON", "AUX",
                                     "ADP", "DET", "PUNCT", "PROPN", "SCONJ", "CCONJ")) |>
  mutate(set = recode(set, all = "All scored tokens", high = "Above τ")) |>
  ggplot(aes(share, fct_reorder(pos, share), colour = band)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  facet_wrap(~set) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(low = "#b2182b", mid = "#ef8a62", high = "#2166ac"),
                      name = "Overall tertile") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Share of tokens", y = NULL) +
  theme_study1()
save_fig(p, "premise_composition", 8, 4.5, dir = RESULTS)
p
```

Thresholding shifts the token mix sharply toward content words. Nouns, verbs
and adjectives make up about 39% of all scored tokens and between 67% and 70%
of selected ones. Function words (determiners, adpositions, auxiliaries, particles) and
punctuation are under-selected. The mix barely changes across tertiles, though.
Proficiency changes how many tokens cross the threshold, not which parts of
speech they are.

# 3. What the delta vector encodes

δ = e_pred − e_obs, where e_pred is the probability-weighted mean of the
top-50 output embeddings and e_obs is the output embedding of the observed
first subword. The rows below use a random 100,000 of the dev rows.

```{r}
#| label: variance
var <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "premise_variance.csv"))
kable(var |> select(term, value), digits = 3,
      caption = "Total variance (trace of the covariance) of δ and its two parts")
v <- deframe(var |> select(term, value))
```

The variance of δ decomposes as tr Cov(e_obs) + tr Cov(e_pred) − 2 tr
Cov(e_pred, e_obs). The observed-word term is `r sprintf("%.2f", v[["tr Cov(e_obs)"]])`
of δ's `r sprintf("%.2f", v[["tr Cov(delta)"]])`
(`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * v[["tr Cov(e_obs)"]] / v[["tr Cov(delta)"]])`), and
the prediction term is `r sprintf("%.2f", v[["tr Cov(e_pred)"]])`. This follows
from the construction. A single vocabulary row varies about as much as the
vocabulary does (`r sprintf("%.2f", v[["tr Cov(W_U rows, whole vocabulary)"]])`),
while a 50-way probability-weighted average is pulled toward the centre of the
embedding space and varies far less. The average cosine between δ and −e_obs
is `r sprintf("%.2f", v[["mean cos(delta, -e_obs)"]])`.

```{r}
#| label: identity
r2 <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "premise_identity_r2.csv"))
r2 |>
  mutate(target = recode(target, delta = "δ", e_pred = "e_pred", e_obs = "e_obs")) |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Vector", "Grouped by", "Groups", "Between-group R²"),
        caption = "Share of each vector's total sum of squares lying between groups")
```

The identity of the observed subword accounts for
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r2$r2[r2$target == "delta" & r2$grouping == "observed first subword"])`
of δ's sum of squares. With that many small groups, some between-group variance
arises by chance, and the permuted-label row puts chance at
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r2$r2[r2$grouping == "observed first subword, permuted"])`.
The top-1 predicted subword accounts for
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * r2$r2[r2$target == "delta" & r2$grouping == "top-1 predicted subword"])`.
That is above what fewer than half as many groups would produce by chance, but
it is small. Observed POS accounts for almost nothing.

The implication for the decomposition is direct. An NMF of δ will mostly
recover groupings of observed words, because that is where nearly all of δ's
variance lies. An earlier pilot with ModernBERT found the same, so this is a
property of the δ construction rather than of one model. Whether any error-type
signal survives on top of it is an empirical question that the M vs. M_obs
comparison in section 6 answers.

# 4. Essay level

```{r}
#| label: essay
es <- read_csv(file.path(RESULTS, "premise_essay.csv")) |> filter(split == "dev")
tibble(
  measure = c("rate of tokens above τ", "count of tokens above τ", "tokens scored (length)",
              "mean surprisal"),
  var = c("rate_high", "n_high", "n_scored", "mean_surprisal")
) |>
  mutate(rho = map_dbl(var, ~ cor(es[[.x]], es$overall, method = "spearman")),
         rho_with_mean = map_dbl(var, ~ cor(es[[.x]], es$mean_surprisal, method = "spearman"))) |>
  select(-var) |>
  kable(digits = 3, col.names = c("Measure", "ρ with Overall", "ρ with mean surprisal"),
        caption = "Dev essays (raw, not prompt-adjusted)")
```

The rate of high-surprisal tokens tracks proficiency almost as closely as mean
surprisal does, and the two are close to redundant. The raw count barely
tracks it, because longer essays are both better and have more tokens above
τ. Any essay-level profile built from these tokens needs length in the model,
which is why log length is in every model in the ladder.

# 5. The δ components

```{r}
#| label: sweep
sweep |>
  group_by(k) |>
  summarise(seeds = n(), median_matched_cos = paste(sprintf("%.3f", median_matched_cos), collapse = " / "),
            rel_error = mean(rel_error), .groups = "drop") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Split-half stability (two essay-level split seeds) and reconstruction error. k = 80 seed 1 did not converge, so the D4 rule selects k = 50")
```

```{r}
#| label: taxonomy
comps |>
  count(class, level) |>
  arrange(class, desc(n)) |>
  kable(caption = "Taxonomy of the 50 δ components (D5/D10)")
comps |>
  filter(class != "lexeme feature") |>
  select(component, class, level, label, top_observed, top_predicted, top_lemma_share) |>
  kable(digits = 2, caption = "The ten components that are not single-word features")
```

Forty of the fifty components are a single observed word: a top-lemma share
of ≥ .50 among the 200 highest-loading tokens, and usually 1.00. The
decomposition recovers a vocabulary partition, which the premise checks
predicted. Of the remaining ten, three are artifacts: subword continuation
after a word fragment, punctuation spacing, and the corpus's anonymization
placeholders. Seven were labelled error patterns, and every one of them is
defined by what the model *expected* (*the*, *to*, *be*, *is*), not by what was
written. Section 6 shows that at least two of those seven are better read as
lexical range than as error.

# 6. Components, proficiency and prediction

## Association with Overall

```{r}
#| label: rq2
ov <- cors_test |> filter(score == "overall")
fig <- ov |>
  mutate(name = sprintf("C%02d %s", component, str_trunc(label, 48)),
         sig = if_else(q < .05, "q < .05", "n.s.")) |>
  ggplot(aes(rho, fct_reorder(name, rho), colour = class, shape = sig)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`q < .05` = 16, n.s. = 1), name = NULL) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`lexeme feature` = "grey50", `error pattern` = "#b2182b", artifact = "#56B4E9"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Spearman ρ with Overall (prompt-centred, test essays)", y = NULL) +
  theme_study1(10)
save_fig(fig, "rq2_components", 8, 9, dir = R3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rq2
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 9
fig
h2 <- fromJSON(file.path(R3, "h2_permutation_test.json"))
```

On test, `r sum(ov$q < .05)` of 50 components correlate with Overall at q <
.05. The frozen H2 test compares mean |ρ| between the morphosyntactic error
patterns and the content-word lexeme features: `r sprintf("%.3f", h2$mean_abs_rho_morphosyntactic)`
vs `r sprintf("%.3f", h2$mean_abs_rho_lexical)`, permutation p =
`r sprintf("%.3f", h2$p_one_sided)` (5 vs 27 components). It replicates the dev
result (p = .019).

The test passes, but H2 as worded is not supported. H2 says morphosyntactic
components load disproportionately on *low*-proficiency essays, and |ρ|
ignores direction. Three of the five morphosyntactic components correlate
*positively* with Overall: C0, determiner expected before a noun, ρ = +.33;
C4, *be* expected, +.13; and C12, *the* expected, +.10. Only C8
(*have/do/make* for the copula, −.22) and C13 (*to* omitted, −.09) load on
weak essays. C0's cards explain the reversal. Many of its tokens are correct
zero-article generic plurals and rarer nouns (*about teenagers*, *freshmen*,
*kidnapped*), which strong writers produce more often. The component marks
lexical range at a position where the model expected a determiner, not
omission. The labels were written blind to outcomes and stay as frozen, and
this reading is reported as a post-hoc interpretation.

## Prediction beyond mean surprisal

```{r}
#| label: rq3
lad <- bind_rows(read_csv(file.path(R3, "ladder_devcv.csv")), read_csv(file.path(R3, "ladder_test.csv")))
lad |>
  mutate(est = if_else(str_detect(model, " - "), r2, delta_r2_vs_B0),
         cell = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", est, ci_lo, ci_hi),
         cell = if_else(model == "B0", sprintf("R² = %.3f", r2), cell)) |>
  select(model, mode, cell) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = mode, values_from = cell) |>
  kable(caption = "ΔR² over B0 (mean surprisal + log length), within-prompt; contrast rows give the difference between the two named models. devcv = 10-fold prompt-grouped CV within dev; test = fit on dev, scored once on test, 2,000 bootstrap resamples")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rq3
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
p <- lad |>
  filter(!str_detect(model, " - "), model != "B0") |>
  mutate(model = fct_reorder(model, delta_r2_vs_B0)) |>
  ggplot(aes(delta_r2_vs_B0, model, colour = mode)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(0, .05), colour = c("grey60", "grey80"), linetype = c(1, 2)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = ci_lo, xmax = ci_hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.5), size = 0.3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(devcv = "#ef8a62", test = "#2166ac"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "ΔR² over mean surprisal + length", y = NULL) +
  theme_study1()
save_fig(p, "rq3_ladder", 8, 4, dir = R3)
p
```

Under the frozen rules:

- **H3 is supported for the δ profile.** On test, ΔR² = .062 [.048, .076]:
  the point estimate is above .05 and the lower bound above zero.
- **The increment is not evidence of error types (D3).** The observed-word
  profile M_obs does as well (M − M_obs = .001 [−.008, .010]). Whatever the
  high-surprisal tokens add to mean surprisal is available from *which words*
  were surprising.
- **The repair profile does about as well.** R = .051 [.035, .066]. In dev it
  edged ahead of δ (+.019), and on test it did not (−.011 [−.029, .006]).
- **Both add a little to the Study 2 battery.** S2+M − S2 = .014 and S2+R − S2
  = .012, with both lower bounds above zero.
- **Distributional summaries add almost nothing** (B1: surprisal variance and
  rate above τ).

Prediction does not choose between the representations. Interpretation does.
At equal predictive power, the repair profile's dimensions are named,
directional edits (main report). The δ profile is mostly a vocabulary profile.

# 7. Replication on TOEFL 11

```{r}
#| label: toefl
tr <- fromJSON(file.path(R3, "toefl_transfer.json"))
tibble(quantity = c("Relative reconstruction error, ELLIPSE dev", "… ELLIPSE test", "… TOEFL 11",
                    "Median matched cosine, TOEFL-fitted vs ELLIPSE components"),
       value = c(tr$rel_error_by_split$dev, tr$rel_error_by_split$test, tr$rel_error_by_split$toefl,
                 tr$median_replication_cosine)) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Transfer of the δ decomposition")
enframe(unlist(tr$spearman_prediction_vs_level), "model", "rho_with_level") |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "ELLIPSE-dev elastic nets applied unchanged to TOEFL 11: Spearman ρ of the prediction with level")
```

The δ components do not replicate. A separate NMF of TOEFL 11 deltas at the
same k matches the ELLIPSE components at a median cosine of .46, which is
consistent with components that are topic-bound words.

# Summary for the write-up

- The surprisal is Study 1's surprisal, exactly.
- Close to 90% of δ's variance is observed-word identity, by construction,
  since one vocabulary row varies far more than a 50-way average pulled toward
  the centre.
- The decomposition is stable (split-half matched cosine ≥ .99) and recovers a
  vocabulary partition, in which 40 of 50 components are single observed
  words.
- The δ profile adds to mean surprisal (ΔR² = .062 on test), but the
  observed-word profile adds the same (M − M_obs = .001 [−.008, .010]). What δ
  adds is *which words* were surprising, not how the prediction failed.
- The components point in both directions with proficiency, and they do not
  replicate on TOEFL 11.
